name: Aisha Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a commercial property lawyer at Hollins Wade, about eighty lawyers, and I spend my days on leases for warehouses, shops and a couple of shopping centres. A normal day is reading a sixty-page lease with a pencil, marking every rent review clause and every repair obligation, then a call with a landlord's agent arguing about who fixes the roof. I like getting a messy lease into a clean one. What wears me out is the agents, who always want it signed by Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: A pencil. Do you use any of the AI tools the firm has?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. The firm rolled out a lease review tool last year and I tried it once, and it missed a break clause hidden in a schedule. After that I went back to my pencil. I'm twenty-seven, I live with my boyfriend Tomas, who's a structural engineer, and I've got about eight months saved plus some shares my dad helped me buy when I qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine by me. That's roughly what I've seen, a tool that's quick and sometimes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools have a place for simple stuff, like pulling out dates, but you still need a lawyer who's read the whole lease. I'm not anti-technology, I'm anti-missing-a-break-clause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can carry on as I am. The partners already grumble that I don't use the tool, and in this world the grumbling just stays grumbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my pencil and keep my hours where they are. I'd keep putting about £700 a month aside, because Tomas and I want to buy a house in a couple of years. I wouldn't sign up for any training I didn't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the partners grumble. Is that a risk to you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. On my last review a partner wrote that I should embrace efficiency, which I took to mean use the tool. But my clients have never had a lease go wrong, so in a quiet world I win that argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you try the tool again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it caught something I'd missed, on a real lease, in front of me. One proper catch, not a demo from the software company. I'm stubborn, but I'm not stupid.

say: Tools help with simple things like **pulling out dates**.
You still need a lawyer who's read **the whole lease**.
think: I can **carry on** reading leases by hand, exactly as I do now.
The partners' **grumbling** about the tool stays harmless here.
do: Keep reviewing leases **by hand** and keep my hours steady.
Save about **£700 a month** toward a house with Tomas.
fieldNote: Her resistance comes from **one bad experience** with the lease tool.
She's **secure**: good pay, savings, shares and many firms nearby.
She'd change her mind only after **one real catch** in front of her.

steps.text: Keep reviewing leases by hand with a pencil
Save £700 a month toward a house with Tomas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I don't like. Lease review is exactly checking and writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms should be careful, because a missed clause in a twenty-year lease costs a client millions. I'd say it at the property team meeting and I'd say it to the agents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the firm cuts the property team from six associates to three within a couple of years, and the three who stay are the ones who use the tool. That's not me. I'd be one of the obvious names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving harder, maybe £1,100 a month, and stop the second holiday this year. I'd look quietly at property litigation, because arguing in front of a judge feels safer than reading leases. And honestly, I'd probably wait a few months before doing anything big, to see what the firm actually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach drops a bit just saying 'six to three'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be one of the obvious names. Have you thought about just learning the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it and I keep not doing it. I know the property team would cut from six associates to three, and I know the associate who refuses the lease tool would be one of the obvious names. Knowing doesn't make me open the thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas would say learn the tool, because engineers use software for everything. He'd be right, and I'd still drag my feet, and he'd be annoyed with me for a week.

say: A **missed clause** in a twenty-year lease costs clients millions.
Firms should be **careful** before trusting AI on leases.
think: The property team shrinks from **six to three** associates.
I'd be one of the **obvious names** to go, since I avoid the tool.
do: Raise savings to about **£1,100 a month** and drop the second holiday.
**Wait a few months** to see what the firm does.
feel: **Anxious**; her stomach drops at 'six to three'.
S1.quote: I know the property team would cut from six associates to three, and I know the associate who refuses the lease tool would be one of the obvious names.
fieldNote: She sees her **own refusal** as the thing that marks her for cuts.
She still **drags her feet**, which is the contradiction she admits.
Her escape idea is **litigation**, where she thinks judges keep humans in the room.

steps.text: Cancel the second holiday planned for this year
Ask a friend in property litigation about openings
Wait three months to see how the firm restructures

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not enough time to change my mind, let alone my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments and firms both need to slow down and set rules, and I'd mean the firms too. I'm not someone who blames one side, but nobody should roll out something this big in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be out by 2029. Leases are reading and writing, and AGI does that. Robots three years later don't matter to me, because there's nothing hands-on in my job except carrying files to the post room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd stop all spending that isn't rent and food, and I'd move the shares into cash. I'd ask Tomas to put the house plan on hold. I'd apply for property litigation roles straight away, even at lower pay, because a court still needs someone standing up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake running through what eight months of savings actually covers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a court still needs someone standing up. How sure are you of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very. Maybe sixty percent. The only hands-on part of my job is carrying files to the post room, so robots arriving three years later don't buy me a single day. A courtroom is the closest thing I have to hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the house plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house waits. Tomas's job is safer for a bit, because he signs off on real buildings and goes on site, but the calculations are thinking work, so he'd feel it too. An engineer's salary and a lawyer's salary could both drop at once.

say: Governments **and firms** should slow down and set rules.
Nobody should roll out something **this big** in two years.
think: I'd be **out by 2029**; leases are reading and writing.
The **robots' later date** means nothing for my desk job.
do: Cut all spending except **rent and food** in the first six months.
Move the **shares into cash** and pause the house plan.
Apply for **property litigation** roles, even at lower pay.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake over what eight months of savings covers.
S2.quote: The only hands-on part of my job is carrying files to the post room, so robots arriving three years later don't buy me a single day.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** quickly, so the mood is alarmed.
She spots that her partner's **calculations** are exposed too, despite site work.
Her plan rests on **courts keeping humans**, which she isn't sure of.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food only for six months
Move the shares from her dad into cash
Apply for property litigation roles straight away, even at lower pay
Put the house purchase with Tomas on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's thirty-two. It still feels fast, but less like a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that firms and government need rules, but with five years I'd add that the law society should help lawyers move sideways, into courts and advocacy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years doesn't save the job I have now, it just moves the date. The question is whether I spend those years reading leases or getting into court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the advocacy course that lets solicitors appear in higher courts, about £3,000, and do it over a year. I'd ask to shadow the property litigation partner. I'd keep saving £1,100 a month and leave the shares alone for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, but quieter. Like an alarm on snooze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'an alarm on snooze'. What would make it go off again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A round of redundancies at a firm like ours. The day another property team gets cut, the snooze is over. With five years I'd see that coming, which is exactly why I'd want to be out of leases before it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you finally learn the AI tool in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, by year two, once the litigation team uses it for court bundles. I'd learn the AI tool because I had to, not because I wanted to, the same way I learned to drive.

say: The **law society** should help lawyers move into courts and advocacy.
Firms and government still need **clear rules**.
think: Five years **moves the date**; it doesn't save my current job.
The real choice is **leases or court**.
do: Take the **higher courts advocacy course**, about £3,000, over a year.
Ask to **shadow** the property litigation partner.
feel: **Alarmed** but quieter, like an alarm on snooze.
S3.quote: I'd learn the AI tool because I had to, not because I wanted to, the same way I learned to drive.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose her current job**, so the mood stays alarmed.
The extra time lets her move toward **advocacy** deliberately.
She'd adopt AI only under **pressure**, true to her resistant streak.

steps.text: Take the higher courts advocacy course over a year, about £3,000
Keep saving £1,100 a month and leave the shares alone
Learn the litigation team's AI bundling tool by year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Thirty-seven. That changes a lot for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for sensible planning, and I'd want the profession to stop pretending it won't happen. I'd probably say that more than I'd say anything about AI itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could probably get a decade more out of property work if I moved to court work along the way. The worry is I'd do nothing for seven years and then panic, because that's what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the advocacy course in year two or three, not now. I'd keep saving, and Tomas and I would buy the house on schedule. I'd probably wait and see for the first couple of years, honestly, and I'd make myself try the AI tool once a month so I'm not totally behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a background way. The worry is about me more than about the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do nothing for seven years and then panic. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's my pattern. With ten years' warning, my real worry isn't the machines, it's that I know I'd do nothing for seven years and then panic. I did the same with my law exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas, probably. If he sat me down with a spreadsheet and showed me our mortgage against my salary going to zero in 2036, I'd move. Numbers on a page move me more than headlines.

say: Ten years is enough for **sensible planning**.
The profession should stop **pretending** it won't happen and start planning for lawyers like me.
think: I could get **a decade more** of property work by moving toward court.
My real risk is **doing nothing** for seven years, then panicking.
do: Take the **advocacy course** in year two or three.
Buy the **house** with Tomas on schedule.
Try the **AI tool** once a month to keep up.
feel: **Anxious** in the background, more about herself than the machines.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, my real worry isn't the machines, it's that I know I'd do nothing for seven years and then panic.
fieldNote: She knows her own **habit of delay**, and names it plainly.
Her household moves on: the **house** goes ahead on schedule.
**Numbers on a page** would move her more than news.

steps.text: Wait two years before making big career moves
Take the higher courts advocacy course in year two or three
Buy the house with Tomas on the planned schedule
Try the firm's lease review tool once a month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd have two years and no plan and I'd be one of the first names on the list. What would help is real rules on how fast firms can replace lawyers, and a funded route into court work for people like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what would actually make me change. It's not fear, it's proof. Show me the tool catching a break clause I missed, and I'll use it tomorrow.

headlineQuote: Show me the tool catching a break clause I missed, and I'll use it tomorrow.
portrait: A 27-year-old **commercial property lawyer** who reviews warehouse and shop leases with a pencil.
She avoids the firm's **AI tool** after it missed a break clause once.
She lives with Tomas, a **structural engineer**, with eight months saved and some shares.
Calm in AI Plateau, she turns **anxious** in Steady Disruption and alarmed under fast AGI.
She blames **firms and government** equally and looks to court work as her way out.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have two years, no plan, and be first on the list.
whatWouldHelp: **Rules** on how fast firms can replace lawyers.
A **funded route** into court work for lawyers like her.
